questions.question: Design a URL shortener service like bit.ly.
questions.title: Design a URL Shortener (bit.ly)
questions.direct_answer: Generate a unique short code per URL using base62 encoding of a distributed ID (Snowflake). Store the mapping in a database with a cache layer for hot URLs. The redirect service resolves short codes to long URLs with sub-10ms p99.

interviewer_intent.testing: Distributed ID generation, caching strategy, redirect performance, and analytics considerations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a random short code without collision detection — use sequential IDs for guaranteed uniqueness
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Snowflake ID encoding to base62, cache-aside pattern for hot URLs, and geographic distribution with CDN

sections.title: The Scale Math That Drives Every Design Decision
sections.content:
A URL shortener seems simple — map a short code to a long URL and redirect. But the scale numbers reveal the real engineering challenges. Bit.ly processes **billions of redirects per month**. At 1 billion redirects/month: **~400 reads/second average**, peaking at **2,000–4,000 reads/second**. If 10 million new URLs are shortened per month, that's **~4 writes/second** — reads dominate by 100:1.

This 100:1 read-to-write ratio drives the entire architecture: the read path must be **sub-10ms** (users click short links in browsers — slow redirects feel broken), which means aggressive caching. The write path can tolerate higher latency since shortening is an explicit API action.

The three core engineering problems: **generating globally unique short codes** without collisions or coordination, **serving redirects** at scale with low latency, and **handling analytics** (click counts, referrers, geography) without slowing down the redirect path. These three problems — unique ID generation, low-latency redirects, and non-blocking analytics — form the architectural backbone of every URL shortener at scale.

sections.title: Short Code Generation: Why Random Strings Are Dangerous
Read Path: Cache-Aside with Redis for Sub-10ms Redirects
Storage, Partitioning, and Geographic Distribution
sections.content:
**Storage estimation:** each URL mapping is approximately 500 bytes (short code + long URL up to 2048 chars + metadata). At 10M new URLs/month × 12 months × 5 years = **600M records × 500 bytes = 300 GB**. This fits comfortably on a single database server, so sharding is unnecessary for storage — but may be needed for read throughput at extreme scale.

The database schema is minimal: `short_code` (primary key, indexed), `long_url`, `created_at`, `user_id`, `expires_at`. Using the short code as the primary key means redirect lookups are primary key reads — the fastest possible database operation.

**Geographic distribution** matters when users are global. A click from Mumbai to a server in Virginia adds 150ms of network latency. Two strategies: **deploy read replicas in multiple regions** with the cache tier (Redis) in each region, so redirects are served locally. Or use a **global CDN with edge caching** — CloudFront can cache redirect responses at edge locations, serving 302s from the nearest POP.

For **custom short domains** (brands wanting `brand.co/xyz`), the system maps domain → tenant and resolves the short code within that tenant's namespace. This is a multi-tenant extension that requires the domain in the cache key: `url:{domain}:{shortCode}`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Base62 encoding of an auto-increment ID** — 6 characters of base62 gives 56 billion unique codes.
- **100:1 read-to-write ratio demands aggressive caching** — cache the short-code → URL mapping in Redis with a 24-hour TTL.
- **301 (permanent) vs 302 (temporary) redirect** — 301 tells browsers to cache the redirect permanently, reducing future load.
- **Cassandra or DynamoDB for the URL store** — single-key lookups by short code; no relational requirements; high read throughput.
- **Custom alias support requires collision detection** — user-provided aliases must check for existence before insertion.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A URL shortener maps short codes to long URLs and redirects users. The scale math shows the real challenge: the system needs to handle 10–100× more reads than writes because every shared link can be clicked millions of times. The architecture must optimize for the redirect hot path.

**Code generation strategy:**
- Base62 encoding of an auto-incrementing database ID is the cleanest approach: characters 0–9, a–z, A–Z give 62 characters; 6 characters gives 56 billion unique codes — more than enough for any realistic service
- Auto-increment IDs are predictable (a feature, not a bug — no collision risk, no retry logic); the database primary key becomes the short code after encoding
- Custom aliases require existence checks before insertion; use `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS` to avoid race conditions on popular custom names

**The read-optimized architecture:**
- With a 100:1 read-to-write ratio, 90%+ of redirect traffic can be served without touching the database; cache the short-code → URL mapping in Redis with a 24-hour TTL
- The CDN layer handles the hottest links: a viral URL clicked 10 million times in an hour hits the CDN edge, which caches the 301 redirect response; origin sees only first-time requests from each CDN PoP
- Cassandra or DynamoDB for the URL store: single-key lookups by short code, high read throughput, no relational requirements — wide-column stores are ideal here

**The 301 vs 302 redirect decision:**
- 301 (Moved Permanently) tells browsers to cache the redirect locally — future clicks go directly to the destination without hitting your service at all; dramatically reduces load but eliminates your ability to count clicks
- 302 (Found/Temporary) forces every redirect through your service — enables click analytics, A/B testing, and link expiration at the cost of one server round-trip per click

I recommend 302 redirects with Redis caching for any service that needs analytics, and 301 only for static marketing links where click tracking has no value and maximum CDN efficiency matters.

items: 5 trillion unique combinations — far more than enough
The question is how to generate them without collisions
Random generation + collision check — generate a random 7-char string, check if it exists in the database, retry on collision
Simple but problematic: as the key space fills up, collision probability increases, and the check requires a database query per attempt
